topic_summary: Lua is a compact, portable, dynamically typed multi-paradigm language designed for embedding and extending host applications. Its small core, tables, first-class functions, closures, metatables, bytecode VM, and C API enable a wide range of programming patterns and integrations.

nodes.label: Lua
nodes.description: Lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm scripting and extension language designed chiefly to be embedded in host applications.

nodes.label: Lua design goals
nodes.description: Portability, speed, extensibility, ease of development, compactness, and a simple embedding interface.

nodes.label: Embedded language
nodes.description: A language supplied as a library/runtime inside another application so that the host can expose customization and scripting.

nodes.label: Extension language
nodes.description: A language used to extend or customize a host program without implementing every domain-specific feature in the core language.

nodes.label: Scripting language
nodes.description: A language commonly used to automate behavior or express application logic within a host runtime.

nodes.label: Multi-paradigm programming
nodes.description: Lua supports procedural, object-oriented/prototype-based, functional, reflective, and metaprogramming techniques.

nodes.label: Imperative programming
nodes.description: A programming style in which statements describe operations and control flow.

nodes.label: Procedural programming
nodes.description: Organizing programs around procedures/functions and explicit sequences of operations.

nodes.label: Functional programming
nodes.description: Programming style enabled in Lua by first-class functions, closures, and higher-order function use.

nodes.label: Reflection and metaprogramming
nodes.description: Language mechanisms allow programs to customize behavior and inspect or influence semantics, notably through metatables.

nodes.label: Dynamic typing
nodes.description: Types are associated with runtime values rather than requiring every variable to have a declared static type.

nodes.label: Strong typing
nodes.description: The source describes Lua as strongly typed while also noting runtime coercion between strings and numbers in supported contexts.

nodes.label: Duck typing
nodes.description: The source metadata characterizes Lua's typing discipline as duck-typed; the article does not formally define that label.

nodes.label: Cross-platform portability
nodes.description: Lua's ANSI C implementation and compact runtime support use across varied host platforms.

nodes.label: ANSI C
nodes.description: The implementation language of the reference Lua implementation.

nodes.label: MIT License
nodes.description: Lua has used the MIT License from version 5.0 onward, according to the article.

nodes.label: Lua file extension
nodes.description: The common Lua source filename extension is .lua.

nodes.label: lua.org
nodes.description: The official Lua website identified in the article metadata.

nodes.label: Reference interpreter
nodes.description: The compact reference implementation of Lua; the article says the compiled interpreter was about 293 kB in the cited context.

nodes.label: Lua virtual machine
nodes.description: Executes Lua bytecode; the source describes Lua 5's VM as register-based.

nodes.label: Lua bytecode
nodes.description: Compiled instruction representation executed by the Lua VM.

nodes.label: Lua compiler
nodes.description: Compiles Lua source text into bytecode, commonly at runtime but also potentially offline.

nodes.label: Runtime compilation
nodes.description: Compilation can occur when code is loaded or executed, making the source-to-bytecode process often invisible to users.

nodes.label: Offline bytecode compilation
nodes.description: Lua bytecode may be produced before deployment to reduce startup/loading work or omit the compiler from the host.

nodes.label: Just-in-time compilation
nodes.description: A JIT compiles code during execution; LuaJIT is identified as a JIT compiler associated with Lua 5.1.

nodes.label: Register-based virtual machine
nodes.description: Lua VM instructions use registers/slots rather than a conventional operand stack architecture, reducing value copying and instruction count per function as described by the source.

nodes.label: CPU
nodes.description: Physical processor that ultimately executes the VM implementation's native machine code.

nodes.label: Host application
nodes.description: The application into which Lua is embedded and whose functions/resources may be exposed to scripts.

nodes.label: Host platform
nodes.description: The operating-system and hardware environment where the host application and Lua runtime execute.

nodes.label: Application customization
nodes.description: Lua's original motivating role: enabling customization of applications when bespoke software changes were needed.

nodes.label: Domain-specific features
nodes.description: Features that can be implemented on top of Lua's small core instead of being built into the base language.

nodes.label: Small extensible core
nodes.description: Lua prefers a small general-purpose core with meta-features over a large fixed set of paradigm-specific features.

nodes.label: Tecgraf
nodes.description: Computer Graphics Technology Group at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro where Lua was created.

nodes.label: Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro
nodes.description: Brazilian university associated with Tecgraf and Lua's creation.

nodes.label: Roberto Ierusalimschy
nodes.description: One of Lua's three creators and a contributor to its design and implementation.

nodes.label: Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo
nodes.description: One of Lua's three creators.

nodes.label: Waldemar Celes
nodes.description: One of Lua's three creators.

nodes.label: Brazilian market reserve
nodes.description: Trade barriers from 1977 to 1992 helped motivate Tecgraf to build tools locally rather than depend on customized foreign software.

nodes.label: Simple Object Language (SOL)
nodes.description: A predecessor data-description/configuration language developed at Tecgraf in 1992–1993.

nodes.label: Data-Entry Language (DEL)
nodes.description: A predecessor data-description/configuration language developed at Tecgraf in 1992–1993.

nodes.label: Petrobras
nodes.description: Company whose engineering projects used earlier Tecgraf interactive graphical programs that motivated more expressive scripting.

nodes.label: Tcl
nodes.description: A 1993 comparison point explicitly designed for embedding; Lua's authors cited Tcl syntax, data-description support, and platform limitations as reasons not to choose it.

nodes.label: Modula
nodes.description: Influenced Lua's control-structure syntax, including if, while, and repeat/until.

nodes.label: CLU
nodes.description: Influenced multiple assignment and multiple return values in Lua.

nodes.label: C++
nodes.description: Listed as an influence on Lua; source also attributes a local-variable declaration idea to C++.

nodes.label: Scheme
nodes.description: Influenced Lua's later semantics, especially anonymous functions and full lexical scoping; also influenced the choice of tables as a primary data structure.

nodes.label: SNOBOL
nodes.description: Influenced Lua syntax and associative-array design, according to the article.

nodes.label: AWK
nodes.description: Influenced Lua's associative-array syntax/design.

nodes.label: LISP
nodes.description: Its single ubiquitous list data structure influenced Lua's decision to use tables as its primary composite structure, according to the cited creators.

nodes.label: Lua creation in 1993
nodes.description: Lua was created in 1993 by Ierusalimschy, de Figueiredo, and Celes at Tecgraf in Brazil.

nodes.label: Lua 1.0
nodes.description: Early Lua design included SOL-derived data-description syntax in its object constructors.

nodes.label: Pre-5.0 license
nodes.description: Versions before Lua 5.0 used a license similar to BSD.

nodes.label: Lua 5.0 and later MIT licensing
nodes.description: Lua switched to the MIT License from version 5.0 onward.

nodes.label: Hello World example
nodes.description: print('Hello, World!') illustrates the concise function-call syntax, including the form without parentheses for a string argument.

nodes.label: Local variable
nodes.description: The local keyword declares a variable whose scope is local to its lexical block.

nodes.label: Single-line comment
nodes.description: A double hyphen begins a comment that continues to the end of the line.

nodes.label: Long comment delimiters
nodes.description: Double square brackets delimit long comments in the shown example.

nodes.label: Long string literal
nodes.description: The source notes double-square-bracket syntax for multi-line strings.

nodes.label: if then end
nodes.description: Lua conditional execution uses if condition then ... end, with all three keywords required.

nodes.label: else branch
nodes.description: Optional alternative branch executed when the if condition is false.

nodes.label: elseif branch
nodes.description: Optional additional conditional branch for multi-condition selection.

nodes.label: while loop
nodes.description: A pre-test loop that repeats while its condition remains true.

nodes.label: repeat-until loop
nodes.description: A post-test loop that executes its body before checking the until condition, analogous to do-while style control.

nodes.label: Numeric for loop
nodes.description: Iterates over a numeric range with start, end, and optional step/delta, which may be negative.

nodes.label: Generic for loop
nodes.description: Iterates over values produced by an iterator function, such as pairs(_G).

nodes.label: Nested loops
nodes.description: Loops may contain other loops, as shown with a grid of rows and values.

nodes.label: Condition expression
nodes.description: Boolean-like expression evaluated to choose a control-flow branch or loop continuation.

nodes.label: ~= operator
nodes.description: The source example uses ~= for inequality.

nodes.label: == operator
nodes.description: The source examples use == to compare values.

nodes.label: Assignment
nodes.description: Assignments bind or update variables and table fields.

nodes.label: Multiple assignment
nodes.description: A feature whose design influence is attributed to CLU.

nodes.label: Multiple return values
nodes.description: Lua functions can return multiple values; the source identifies CLU as an influence on this design.

nodes.label: Numbers
nodes.description: The source describes numbers as including double-precision floating point and 64-bit integers by default in the stated version context.

nodes.label: Boolean values
nodes.description: One of Lua's small set of atomic value types.

nodes.label: Strings
nodes.description: Lua strings are atomic values and support the length operator in the source example.

nodes.label: nil
nodes.description: Special value used for absent table entries and also prohibited as a table key.

nodes.label: NaN
nodes.description: NaN is not permitted as a table key according to the source.

nodes.label: Runtime coercion
nodes.description: Lua supports automatic conversion between string and number values at runtime in supported contexts.

nodes.label: Garbage collection
nodes.description: Lua automatically manages the lifetime of objects such as closures, reducing the need for manual reference counting in embedded C code.

nodes.label: Proper tail calls
nodes.description: Listed as an advanced language feature in the source.

nodes.label: Coroutines
nodes.description: Lua supports coroutines for cooperative multitasking.

nodes.label: Dynamic module loading
nodes.description: Lua supports loading modules dynamically.

nodes.label: Function
nodes.description: Functions are first-class values that can be assigned, passed, returned, and replaced.

nodes.label: First-class functions
nodes.description: Functions can be stored in variables/tables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions, and redefined through references.

nodes.label: Anonymous function
nodes.description: A function expression without a named declaration, shown as the return value of addto.

nodes.label: Lexical scoping
nodes.description: A function resolves captured variables according to the lexical scope where it was defined.

nodes.label: Closure
nodes.description: A function bundled with access to variables from its lexical environment; each addto call yields a closure over its own x.

nodes.label: Upvalue
nodes.description: Bytecode metadata uses the term upvalues for external lexical variables referenced by a function.

nodes.label: Function redefinition
nodes.description: The example saves print in oldprint and replaces print, demonstrating that function values can be rebound.

nodes.label: return statement
nodes.description: Returns one or more values from a function.

nodes.label: Table
nodes.description: Lua's only built-in composite data type in the article; a heterogeneous associative array that underpins arrays, records, namespaces, and user-defined types.

nodes.label: Associative array
nodes.description: Key-value structure used for table storage, with heterogeneous values and keys except nil and NaN.

nodes.label: Table constructor
nodes.description: Curly braces create a table and can initialize key-value or sequence entries.

nodes.label: Table reference semantics
nodes.description: Tables are passed by reference/call-by-sharing; aliases observe changes to the same table object.

nodes.label: Table key
nodes.description: A table key may be any value except nil and NaN, including functions.

nodes.label: Table field access
nodes.description: t.x is syntactic sugar for t['x'] when accessing a string-keyed table field.

nodes.label: Array-like table
nodes.description: Tables can serve as arrays using numeric keys; automatically assigned sequence indexes start at 1.

nodes.label: One-based indexing
nodes.description: Lua's automatic array-style indexing starts at 1, although explicit index 0 is legal.

nodes.label: Length operator #
nodes.description: The # operator is used for strings and tables; for tables with holes, the article describes the length result as potentially ambiguous.

nodes.label: Table hole
nodes.description: A nil gap in numeric table indices makes the table length operator's result potentially non-unique.

nodes.label: Nested tables
nodes.description: Tables can contain tables, enabling grids and multidimensional structures.

nodes.label: Record-like table
nodes.description: String keys let a table represent a record with named fields.

nodes.label: Namespace table
nodes.description: A table containing related functions can emulate a namespace.

nodes.label: Metatable
nodes.description: A metatable customizes table behavior and supports extension of Lua's semantics.

nodes.label: setmetatable
nodes.description: Associates a metatable with a table, enabling lookup delegation and metamethod behavior.

nodes.label: __index metamethod
nodes.description: A missing-key lookup can invoke a function or delegate to a table through __index.

nodes.label: Memoization
nodes.description: The Fibonacci example caches computed values in a table so later lookups reuse them.

nodes.label: Operator overloading
nodes.description: Metatables may define metamethods such as __add and __sub to customize operators.

nodes.label: Metamethod
nodes.description: Named hooks in a metatable that customize operations or lookup semantics.

nodes.label: Object-oriented programming
nodes.description: Lua supports object-oriented designs using tables and functions without a built-in class construct.

nodes.label: Prototype-based object model
nodes.description: Objects can delegate missing methods and fields to a prototype table via metatable lookup.

nodes.label: Class emulation
nodes.description: Programmers may emulate class-like APIs using tables, constructors, methods, and metatables; Lua does not have built-in classes according to the article.

nodes.label: self parameter
nodes.description: Colon method syntax supplies the receiver as an implicit first parameter named self.

nodes.label: Colon method syntax
nodes.description: function t:method(...) and object:method(...) are syntactic sugar for explicit receiver passing.

nodes.label: Inheritance emulation
nodes.description: Single and multiple inheritance can be emulated with metatables and delegated lookup.

nodes.label: Multiple inheritance
nodes.description: The source states that multiple inheritance can be implemented; __index may be a function or table.

nodes.label: Vector example
nodes.description: The article's Vector example demonstrates constructor tables, metatables, methods, fields, and colon syntax.

nodes.label: VectorMult example
nodes.description: The derived VectorMult example shows prototype-style inheritance and a mutating multiply method.

nodes.label: Lua C API
nodes.description: Minimal API for embedding Lua in C applications and exposing host functionality to scripts.

nodes.label: Lua core library
nodes.description: Core part of the C API, with lua_* functions.

nodes.label: Lua auxiliary library
nodes.description: Auxiliary C API, with luaL_* helpers and macros that simplify more complex operations.

nodes.label: C API stack
nodes.description: Lua's C API uses a stack to exchange values and arguments between C and Lua; indices can be positive or negative.

nodes.label: Positive stack index
nodes.description: Positive C API indices count from the bottom/oldest values in the stack.

nodes.label: Negative stack index
nodes.description: Negative C API indices are offsets from the top; -1 refers to the topmost, most recently pushed value.

nodes.label: lua_State
nodes.description: Opaque state/context used by the C API; created with luaL_newstate in the example.

nodes.label: luaL_newstate
nodes.description: Creates a Lua state in the C embedding example.

nodes.label: luaL_dostring
nodes.description: Loads and executes a string containing Lua code in the C API example.

nodes.label: lua_getglobal
nodes.description: Pushes a named global value onto the Lua C API stack in the example.

nodes.label: lua_pushinteger
nodes.description: Pushes an integer argument onto the C API stack.

nodes.label: lua_call
nodes.description: Calls a Lua function using arguments pushed onto the stack and requests a return value.

nodes.label: lua_tointeger
nodes.description: Converts the top stack value to an integer in the example.

nodes.label: lua_pop
nodes.description: Removes stack values after use in the C API example.

nodes.label: lua_close
nodes.description: Closes a Lua state and releases associated runtime resources in the example.

nodes.label: _G globals table
nodes.description: Main global namespace table; earlier versions used LUA_GLOBALSINDEX in the API.

nodes.label: Lua registry
nodes.description: Special registry table accessible through LUA_REGISTRYINDEX for C programs to retain Lua values.

nodes.label: Manual reference counting
nodes.description: The article contrasts Lua's C API with APIs requiring manual reference counting.

nodes.label: Native extension module
nodes.description: Shared object that exposes native facilities to Lua scripts through the C API.

nodes.label: luaopen_foo entry point
nodes.description: When a C library is loaded through require('foo'), Lua calls luaopen_foo, which generally returns a table of methods.

nodes.label: require
nodes.description: Loads a module written in Lua or a native extension module.

nodes.label: package.loadlib
nodes.description: Alternative mechanism identified for loading extension modules.

nodes.label: LuaRocks
nodes.description: Package-management system providing a growing set of reusable Lua modules ('rocks').

nodes.label: Language bindings
nodes.description: Bindings connect Lua with other programming languages; the article notes bindings for many languages and template/generator approaches for C++.

nodes.label: string.dump
nodes.description: The source mentions the string library dump function as a way to produce bytecode.

nodes.label: load/loadstring/loadfile
nodes.description: Functions identified as ways to load or execute bytecode/code from within Lua; names differ across Lua versions.

nodes.description: Core standard-library modules that are extended by native or Lua modules.

nodes.label: Game engine
nodes.description: A host application that embeds a scripting runtime to expose game logic, customization, or modding APIs.

nodes.label: Script sandbox
nodes.description: A constrained execution environment intended to limit what embedded scripts can access; Luau is specifically described as improving sandboxing for untrusted code.

nodes.label: Host-exposed API
nodes.description: Functions and objects made available by a host application to scripts.

nodes.label: Garbage collector runtime
nodes.description: Runtime component that tracks managed objects such as closures and reclaims memory when no longer needed.

nodes.label: Native machine code
nodes.description: Machine instructions executed directly by a CPU, distinct from Lua bytecode interpreted or compiled by the runtime.

nodes.label: Lua source script
nodes.description: Textual Lua program that is compiled to bytecode before VM execution.

nodes.label: Module search and loading
nodes.description: Runtime process that resolves require requests and loads Lua or native modules.

nodes.label: C/Lua value marshalling
nodes.description: Values are transferred between C and Lua through stack operations and conversion functions.

nodes.label: Cooperative multitasking
nodes.description: Coroutines provide cooperative rather than automatically preemptive task switching, according to the source's characterization.

nodes.label: Principle of least privilege
nodes.description: Lexical scoping can enforce fine-grained information hiding, supporting the principle of least privilege.

nodes.label: Portability versus host integration
nodes.description: A compact ANSI C runtime and C API favor broad portability and embedding, while platform-specific host bindings still determine available capabilities.

nodes.label: Source-to-VM execution pipeline
nodes.description: Source text is compiled to bytecode; the VM executes bytecode. Compilation may happen at runtime or offline, and JIT implementations may compile code to native instructions.

nodes.label: Embedded-language integration model
nodes.description: The host creates a Lua state and uses the C API to load scripts and exchange values, enabling extension without moving the entire application into Lua.

nodes.label: C API call stack model
nodes.description: The C API stack is the transfer mechanism for arguments and results; the example calls foo(5,3) and reads 8.

nodes.label: Table-based object model
nodes.description: An object's table stores its fields; metatable lookup delegates missing methods to a prototype table.

nodes.label: Table reference and aliasing model
nodes.description: Both variables refer to the same table object, so a field mutation is visible through both references.

nodes.label: Closure capture model
nodes.description: Each invocation of addto creates a function retaining access to that invocation's x value.

nodes.label: Metatable-driven memoization
nodes.description: A metatable's __index function handles missing keys and writes computed values into the table.

nodes.label: Lua control-flow selection
nodes.description: Explicit then/end delimit conditional blocks, while optional else/elseif supply alternatives.

nodes.label: Lua loop families
nodes.description: Lua provides four loop forms in the article's taxonomy, each suited to different termination or iteration logic.

nodes.label: Table as universal composite data model
nodes.description: The same table primitive represents heterogeneous associative arrays, sequences, records, nested structures, namespaces, and object fields.

nodes.label: Lua module loading model
nodes.description: Lua's module system can load Lua modules or native shared objects; native modules conventionally expose luaopen_foo.

nodes.label: Managed object lifetime
nodes.description: Lua garbage collection manages objects such as closures and avoids requiring the host C program to manually reference-count every Lua object.

nodes.label: Lua dialect and target-language relationships
nodes.description: Luau, Ravi, Teal, Pluto, GLua, PICO-8 Lua, LuaJIT and other variants differ in compatibility, typing, syntax, performance or host-specific APIs.

nodes.label: Historical influence graph
nodes.description: Lua's design emerged from practical embedding requirements and selective borrowing from earlier languages rather than adopting a single paradigm wholesale.

nodes.label: Game scripting integration
nodes.description: Lua's embedding design allows game developers to expose scriptable behavior while retaining core engine functionality in native code.

nodes.label: Lua typing profile
nodes.description: The article characterizes base Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed while also describing coercion; dialects such as Luau and Ravi add other typing features.

nodes.label: Bytecode precompilation and loading
nodes.description: The article describes string.dump and load-family functions, as well as offline compilation to reduce load time or omit the compiler.

nodes.label: Namespace via table
nodes.description: A table containing related functions can act as a namespace without requiring a dedicated namespace construct.

nodes.label: Prototype inheritance via metatables
nodes.description: Metatable delegation makes inherited methods visible without copying them into each object.

nodes.label: Source Bytecode

nodes.label: Vm Cpu
nodes.description: The Lua VM executes bytecode as a software runtime; the CPU executes native instructions implementing that runtime.

nodes.label: Register Stack Vm
nodes.description: Lua's VM is described as register-based, while the C API used to exchange values is stack-based; these are different layers and do not conflict.

nodes.label: Dynamic Static

nodes.label: Table Array
nodes.description: An array is a usage pattern of a general key-value table, not a separate built-in composite type.

nodes.label: Table Alias Copy
nodes.description: Assigning a table variable copies a reference; creating a new table constructor creates a distinct table.

nodes.label: Nil Hole
nodes.description: nil denotes an absent table value; a nil gap in a sequence can make the # length result ambiguous.

nodes.label: Field Syntax
nodes.description: Dot syntax is shorthand for a string-key lookup and does not introduce a separate field-storage mechanism.

nodes.label: Function Closure
nodes.description: A closure is a function that retains access to lexical variables from its defining environment.

nodes.label: Prototype Class
nodes.description: Lua's examples use prototype delegation; class-like APIs are programmer-built conventions rather than a built-in class construct.

nodes.label: Metatable Metamethod
nodes.description: A metatable is the table of customization rules; a metamethod is a named hook such as __index or __add.

nodes.label: Coroutine Thread
nodes.description: Coroutines provide cooperative task switching; the source does not describe them as operating-system threads.

nodes.label: Jit Interpreter
nodes.description: The baseline execution model compiles to VM bytecode; a JIT is an implementation technique that can compile code during execution.

nodes.label: Core Aux
nodes.description: The core API provides base functionality; the auxiliary library supplies helper operations and macros.

nodes.label: Lua Luau

nodes.label: Native Lua Module

nodes.label: Table Namespace

nodes.label: Source Claim Synthesis

nodes.label: Version Dialect

source_claims.claim: Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm language designed mainly for embedding in applications.
Lua was created in 1993 at Tecgraf by Roberto Ierusalimschy, Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo, and Waldemar Celes.
SOL and DEL were predecessor configuration/data-description languages whose limitations motivated a more expressive language.
Lua favors a small base language and extensible meta-features over a large set of paradigm-specific built-ins.
Tables are Lua's only built-in composite type and support associative arrays, records, arrays, namespaces, and objects.
First-class functions, lexical scoping, and closures support higher-order programming and information hiding.
Metatables customize table behavior and enable lookup delegation, memoization, operator overloading, and object-oriented patterns.
Lua source is compiled to bytecode for a register-based virtual machine; compilation may occur at runtime or offline.
The C API is stack-based and provides core and auxiliary libraries for embedding and calling Lua from C.
Lua can load Lua modules and native shared-object extensions, with LuaRocks providing package management.
Lua is widely used in game development due to its embeddability, execution speed, and short learning curve.
The article lists non-game applications such as Lightroom, LuaTeX, Redis, Neovim, Nginx, Wireshark, and MediaWiki Scribunto.
Lua has derivatives and dialects that differ in typing, performance, syntax, compatibility, and host integration.
Lua versions before 5.0 used a BSD-like license; versions from 5.0 onward use the MIT License.
The article says the register-based VM can reduce value copying and the number of instructions per function compared with stack-based VM architectures.
Luau is described as a Lua 5.1 derivative with gradual typing, performance focus, and improved sandboxing for untrusted scripts.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Embedding describes how the runtime is integrated into a host; extension describes the purpose of allowing users to add behavior to that host.
Lua source is human-readable text; bytecode is the compiled VM instruction representation.
The Lua VM executes bytecode as a software runtime; the CPU executes native instructions implementing that runtime.
Lua's VM is described as register-based, while the C API used to exchange values is stack-based; these are different layers and do not conflict.
Base Lua is described as dynamically typed; Luau adds gradual typing as a dialect feature.
An array is a usage pattern of a general key-value table, not a separate built-in composite type.
Assigning a table variable copies a reference; creating a new table constructor creates a distinct table.
nil denotes an absent table value; a nil gap in a sequence can make the # length result ambiguous.
Dot syntax is shorthand for a string-key lookup and does not introduce a separate field-storage mechanism.
A closure is a function that retains access to lexical variables from its defining environment.
Lua's examples use prototype delegation; class-like APIs are programmer-built conventions rather than a built-in class construct.
A metatable is the table of customization rules; a metamethod is a named hook such as __index or __add.
Coroutines provide cooperative task switching; the source does not describe them as operating-system threads.
The baseline execution model compiles to VM bytecode; a JIT is an implementation technique that can compile code during execution.
The core API provides base functionality; the auxiliary library supplies helper operations and macros.
Luau derives from Lua 5.1 and adds dialect-specific typing, performance, and sandbox features; it is not identical to every Lua version.
require is the loading interface; a native extension is a compiled shared object that exposes an entry point such as luaopen_foo.
A namespace table is a programming convention built using a general table, not a dedicated namespace primitive.
Source claims capture what the article states; formal models may organize those statements into explanatory pipelines.
A named stable Lua version and an implementation targeting an older language version are different kinds of release identity.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua has separate built-in array, record, and object composite types.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes tables as the only built-in composite type; arrays, records, namespaces, and objects are patterns built with tables.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua has native class declarations like class-based languages.
misconceptions.correction: The article says Lua has no built-in class concept in the described model; class-like behavior is emulated with tables, functions, and metatables.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua source text is executed directly without compilation.
misconceptions.correction: The article states that Lua source is compiled into bytecode that runs on the Lua VM.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua's VM and C API both use the same stack architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The VM is described as register-based, whereas the C API uses a stack to exchange values.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua's automatic sequence indexing starts at zero.
misconceptions.correction: The source says automatic array-style indexing starts at 1, although explicit key 0 is legal.

misconceptions.misconception: The # operator always returns an unambiguous count for any table.
misconceptions.correction: The article notes that tables with holes can have more than one valid boundary for the length operator.

misconceptions.misconception: Assigning one table variable to another clones the table.
misconceptions.correction: The source example shows both variables referring to the same table; mutation through one is visible through the other.

misconceptions.misconception: Metatables are only for object-oriented programming.
misconceptions.correction: The source shows metatables also supporting missing-key lookup, memoization, operator overloading, and semantic customization.

misconceptions.misconception: A returned function loses access to its outer local when the outer call returns.
misconceptions.correction: The closure example retains access to its own captured x value, managed by the garbage collector.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua is used only for games.
misconceptions.correction: The article lists editors, web servers, databases, packet analyzers, typesetting, and MediaWiki among non-game uses.

misconceptions.misconception: Luau, LuaJIT, Teal, and standard Lua are identical implementations.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes dialects/implementations with different compatibility, typing, performance, syntax, or sandbox behavior.

misconceptions.misconception: Embedding Lua requires manual reference counting for every Lua object.
misconceptions.correction: The article explicitly contrasts Lua's C API with APIs that require manual reference counting.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic typing necessarily means weak typing.
misconceptions.correction: The source metadata describes Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed, and separately lists supported runtime coercion; these labels are not synonyms.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua includes every advanced feature as a fixed built-in construct.
misconceptions.correction: The design emphasizes small extensible meta-features, with classes and inheritance implemented by conventions rather than dedicated constructs.

misconceptions.misconception: Coroutines automatically provide preemptive parallel threads.
misconceptions.correction: The source characterizes coroutines as cooperative multitasking; it does not claim OS-thread parallelism.
